payload.throughline: Read the display, characterize uncertainty, bound the conclusion, and project only as far as the observed pattern warrants.

learner_content_blocks: Low-stakes prerequisite boundary: Read labeled variables and units, and perform the arithmetic needed for a simple ratio or average. If either prerequisite is insecure, use the packet-declared handoff.
Starting observation: A sample has values 4, 5, 5, 6, and 30. Which statistic best describes a typical value without being pulled strongly by 30?
This response cannot select a route, satisfy an exit, or establish mastery.

Goal: turn a display into a precise statement about pattern, center, spread, and representation fit before drawing any explanation. If a prerequisite check is insecure, pause rather than guess and use the exact handoff: V3-LES-264240 via V3-EDG-805112 + R14-SM-001; V3-LES-765609 via V3-EDG-609972 + V3-EDG-685845 + R14-SM-002.
Start with labels, units, comparison groups, and sample sizes. Describe direction or difference only after confirming what each mark represents.

Mean uses every value and is sensitive to extremes; median is the ordered middle; mode is most frequent. Range spans minimum to maximum, interquartile range spans the middle half, and standard deviation summarizes typical distance from the mean. Match the statistic and display to the question.
Use four passes: label, center, spread, fit. A graph can reveal shape or trend, a table preserves exact values, and a data list permits direct calculation.

I ask what comparison the prompt requires. If one extreme value pulls the mean away from most observations, I choose median for typical value. If the question is variability around the mean, I use standard deviation rather than range alone.
A response-time list is 8, 9, 9, 10, and 24 seconds. The mean is 12 seconds, the median is 9 seconds, the mode is 9 seconds, and the range is 16 seconds.
Because one slow response pulls the mean upward, the median better represents the typical observation. A dot plot would also reveal the isolated high value more clearly than a single mean.
Guided practice: label the comparison, compute one center and one spread, then state why those summaries fit.
Less support: choose the statistic that answers a fresh question and justify the representation.
On your own: interpret a new display without an answer-bearing cue.
Boundary: a lower mean does not prove every observation is lower, and overlapping ranges do not erase a difference in medians. Description is not causal explanation.
Near exit: identify a supported pattern and the summary statistic that expresses it.
Changed exit: move between a graph and a skewed data list, selecting a center-and-spread pair that remains informative.
Repair the summary function: copy the values, order them, compute the requested center, then compute the spread named in the prompt.
Fresh re-entry: summarize an unexposed data set with new values and units.
Repair representation fit: name the decisive feature—exact values, distribution shape, category comparison, or time trend—then choose the display or statistic that preserves it.
Fresh changed re-entry: choose a fitting representation and summary for a new skewed data set.
Recap: labels establish meaning; center and spread characterize the data; representation fit determines what pattern can be read safely.
Low-stakes prerequisite boundary: Identify the measured variable, comparison groups, and direction of a difference before interpreting error bars or intervals.
Starting observation: A thermometer reads 2 degrees Celsius too high for every calibration bath. Which error is most directly indicated?
This response cannot select a route, satisfy an exit, or establish mastery.

Goal: classify error and read uncertainty without turning a statistical result into certainty. If a prerequisite check is insecure, pause rather than guess and use the exact handoff: V3-LES-264240 via V3-EDG-805112 + R14-SM-001; V3-LES-765609 via V3-EDG-609972 + V3-EDG-685845 + R14-SM-002.

Random error makes repeated measurements vary unpredictably and can often be reduced by repeated independent measurements. Systematic error shifts measurements in a consistent direction and is not repaired merely by repetition.

An estimate carries uncertainty. A confidence interval gives a range produced by a stated procedure; statistical significance addresses compatibility with a specified null model at a chosen threshold, not practical importance or proof that an explanation is true.
Random error widens a cloud; systematic error moves the whole cloud. An interval fences plausible estimate values under the stated procedure, not every possible truth.

I inspect whether measurements scatter on both sides or share one offset. For intervals, I report the observed estimate and uncertainty, then avoid claiming certainty, mechanism, or importance unless supplied.
A balance reads every certified 100.0-gram mass as about 103.0 grams, while repeated readings vary only slightly.
The consistent positive offset is systematic error. Taking many more readings would estimate the shifted value precisely but would not remove the calibration bias.
Guided practice: locate the error pattern and state what repetition or calibration can and cannot fix.
Less support: interpret a fresh interval without converting it into certainty.
On your own: distinguish uncertainty from a causal or practical claim.
Boundary: small random spread does not guarantee accuracy, and statistical significance does not establish a large or important effect.
Near exit: classify random versus systematic error from repeated measurements.
Changed exit: interpret a confidence-interval comparison and preserve the uncertainty language.
Repair the error-type function: ask whether repeated values scatter unpredictably or move together in one direction relative to a reference.
Fresh re-entry: classify an unexposed measurement pattern with a new instrument and units.
Repair interval interpretation: state estimate, interval, and comparison target separately; do not replace compatibility language with certainty.
Fresh changed re-entry: interpret a new interval table without overclaiming effect size or cause.
Recap: random error spreads, systematic error shifts, and every significance or interval statement remains bounded by its procedure and uncertainty.
Low-stakes prerequisite boundary: State the observed comparison and its uncertainty before evaluating a conclusion.
Starting observation: In an observational sample, higher sleep duration is associated with higher quiz scores. Which conclusion is supported?
This response cannot select a route, satisfy an exit, or establish mastery.

Goal: choose the strongest conclusion the presented evidence supports—no weaker than necessary and no stronger than warranted. If a prerequisite check is insecure, pause rather than guess and use the exact handoff: V3-LES-264240 via V3-EDG-805112 + R14-SM-001; V3-LES-765609 via V3-EDG-609972 + V3-EDG-685845 + R14-SM-002.
Break a candidate conclusion into clauses. Each consequential clause needs a corresponding result, comparison, and uncertainty statement.
A plausible alternative explanation limits causal or exclusive language unless the design or results address it. Outside-background speculation and policy recommendations remain outside this KC.
Use an evidence leash: every claim clause must stay connected to a displayed observation. If the leash breaks, the conclusion overreaches.
I prefer precise verbs such as was associated with or differed under these conditions. I reject caused, always, or only when the design and data do not rule out alternatives.
In an observational data set, people who reported more weekly walking also reported lower resting heart rate.
A supported conclusion is that walking reports and resting heart rate were associated in this sample. The data alone do not show that walking caused the difference or exclude another variable.
Guided conclusion check: underline each claim clause and point to the result that supports it.
Less support: identify one plausible alternative before selecting the bounded conclusion.
On your own: reject causal, universal, or policy language unsupported by the results.
Boundary: a conclusion may be cautious yet still unsupported, or bold yet supported. The deciding test is the evidence link, not tone.
Near exit: choose the strongest supported conclusion from a familiar result pattern.
Changed exit: compare two data sources and retain a plausible alternative while rejecting an exclusive explanation.
Repair the evidence boundary: split the conclusion into clauses and delete or soften every clause with no matching result.
Fresh re-entry: select a bounded conclusion for an unexposed study result.
Repair alternatives: name at least one other variable or design feature consistent with the results, then remove exclusive causal language.
Fresh changed re-entry: choose a conclusion that fits a new multi-source result while preserving alternatives.
Recap: match every clause to evidence, preserve plausible alternatives, and keep speculation or policy outside the conclusion.
Low-stakes prerequisite boundary: Identify the observed pattern and the range or conditions in which it was established before making a prediction.
Starting observation: Mean output is 20 units at setting A and 31 units at setting B. A new trial repeats setting B under similar conditions. Which prediction is most bounded?
This response cannot select a route, satisfy an exit, or establish mastery.

Goal: project a data-supported implication only as far as the observed pattern and stated change permit. If a prerequisite check is insecure, pause rather than guess and use the exact handoff: V3-LES-264240 via V3-EDG-805112 + R14-SM-001; V3-LES-765609 via V3-EDG-609972 + V3-EDG-685845 + R14-SM-002.
A bounded replication predicts what should happen when the relevant observed conditions repeat. It carries the direction and approximate relation, not an exact guaranteed value.
For a changed condition, identify which model link the change affects. Preserve unchanged links, revise the affected implication, and stop before unobserved ranges or policy recommendations.
Extend with guardrails: start at the last supported point, name the new condition, carry only the established relation, and attach an uncertainty stop sign.
I ask whether this is a repeat within the observed range or a changed condition. I reject exact guarantees, limitless trends, and recommendations that the data never tested.
Across 10, 20, and 30 minutes of practice, average accuracy rises from 60% to 68% to 75%. A new group repeats the 20-minute condition.
A bounded prediction is that its average may be near the previously observed 68% under comparable conditions. The pattern does not guarantee 68% or justify extrapolating to many hours.
Guided projection: name the repeated or changed condition and carry forward only the observed relation.
Less support: choose a bounded implication without an exact-value guarantee.
On your own: reject unobserved-range extrapolation and policy language.
Boundary: prediction is not prophecy. A trend within three points does not license indefinite linear growth.
Near exit: predict a repeat within an observed range.
Changed exit: revise the implication when one condition changes while other relations remain.
Repair replication: match the new case to the nearest observed condition and use approximate, conditional language.
Fresh re-entry: predict a new repeat from an unexposed pattern.
Repair changed-condition reasoning: mark the changed variable, identify the model link it affects, and preserve every link the change leaves untouched.
Fresh changed re-entry: project a bounded implication for a new altered condition.
Recap: repeat within range, revise for changed conditions, preserve uncertainty, and stop before unbounded or policy claims.
